# Answer key - Chapter 08: DevSecOps, WAF and secure applications {.unnumbered}

<!-- Source-only: this directory is excluded from the render in _quarto.yml
     ("!answers/"). Never link these files from a chapter. Numbering must
     match the chapter's Self-check section 1:1. -->

**Q1** *(tests @sec-08-application-security · basic)* - **Correct: b.**
The chapter states the SBOM "answers the one question that matters during an
incident: whether and where the library is in use"; the Log4Shell callout
illustrates the same point - a, c and d are questions the SBOM does not
address.

**Q2** *(tests @sec-08-secure-development-lifecycle · basic)* - **Correct: c.**
STRIDE sorts threats into Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information
disclosure, Denial of service and Elevation of privilege, turning the
open-ended threat question of Session 1 into a checklist; a describes canary
deployment, b describes part of SAST, d is invented.

**Q3** *(tests @sec-08-devsecops-pipeline · basic)* - **Accepted answers:**
"canary deployment sends the new version to a small fraction of users first
and observes before rolling on"; "blue/green deployment keeps two
environments so that a release can be switched over, and back, instantly"
(any phrasing with small-fraction-first for canary and two switchable
environments for blue/green).

**Q4** *(tests @sec-08-devsecops-pipeline · basic)* - **Correct: a.**
The chapter places SAST in continuous integration (so vulnerable code does
not merge) and DAST in continuous delivery against the staged application
(CSA, 2024, pp. 243–245); c reverses them, b and d misplace both.

**Q5** *(tests @sec-08-devsecops-pipeline · basic)* - **Accepted answers:**
"an imperative specification lists the steps to perform; a declarative one
states the desired end state and lets the tooling reach it" (any phrasing
that pairs steps-to-perform with desired-end-state; a bonus is noting the
Kubernetes work-towards-a-goal comparison).

**Q6** *(tests @sec-08-waf · basic)* - **Correct: d.**
The Guidance treats the WAF as a control that prevents attacks from
arriving, not a repair for flawed applications or an excuse for careless
development (CSA, 2024, p. 247); a is the excuse the Guidance rejects, b
confuses the Session 4 distinction (NGFW broad, WAF one application), and c
describes a network firewall, not a Layer 7 control.

**Q7 - applied scenario** *(tests @sec-08-exercises · applied)* -
**Model answer:** First hours: the SBOM has already answered where the
library is in use, so no time is lost searching (the Log4Shell lesson);
the WAF in front of Nextcloud is the runtime control that limits
exploitation now - it inspects incoming HTTP requests and blocks those
matching the attack pattern even though the flaw is present (@def-waf,
runtime-defence phase of the SSDLC). Following days: when the patched
library or plugin version appears, the change goes through the DevSecOps
pipeline - dependency scanning/software composition analysis confirms the
new version, SAST runs in CI, DAST probes the staged application in CD
(@def-devsecops) - and because the infrastructure is immutable and defined
as code, the environment is rebuilt fresh from the tested definition, so
what was tested is exactly what runs, with no drift. **Grading notes:**
full credit requires (1) SBOM for locating the exposure, (2) WAF as the
interim runtime shield, (3) the patched version delivered through the
pipeline with its automated tests, and (4) the immutability/no-drift
argument; partial credit for three of the four; naming the layers as
independent defence in depth (the WAF catches what the pipeline missed)
earns the last point.

## Sketch answers to the chapter exercises

(1) *(@exr-08-shifting-left - Shifting left)*
Shifting left moves security work earlier in the lifecycle (design and
build rather than production); a flaw caught in design is fixed by changing a
plan, while the same flaw in production may mean an incident, an emergency
patch and lost data.

(2) *(@exr-08-sast-vs-dast - SAST vs DAST)*
SAST examines source code before deployment to find
flaws; DAST probes the running application from outside afterwards. Each has a
blind spot, SAST seeing code but not behaviour and DAST behaviour but not
code, so they are combined, as symmetric and asymmetric encryption are in
Session 6.

(3) *(@exr-08-devsecops-adds - What DevSecOps adds)*
DevSecOps embeds automated security checks (SAST in CI, DAST in
CD) into every change rather than an occasional gate; because immutable
infrastructure builds every environment fresh from one tested definition,
there is no drift between what was tested and what runs.

(4) *(@exr-08-ngfw-vs-waf - NGFW vs WAF, revisited)*
An NGFW secures
the network broadly with application awareness; a WAF secures one web
application by inspecting HTTP requests; the WAF blocks the SQL-injection
attempt.

(5) *(@exr-08-disclosed-library-flaw - A disclosed library flaw)*
A software bill of materials (SBOM) shows whether and where the
library is used; a web application firewall could block exploitation of the
flaw at runtime even if the vulnerable library is present.
